prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B008 as a single part, Katori and Ye. After the first round the case rests on three things I can weigh as an experimentalist. First, the invention is a specific, testable idea: a magic wavelength at which the lattice shifts both clock levels equally, so that many neutral atoms can be held without perturbing the transition. Second, the performance claim has been independently reproduced and surpassed (Sr, Yb, Hg; JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) and is checked in routine comparisons, which is the reproducibility standard I apply to any claim. Third, the capability already yields measurements that were not possible before, such as gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample and spin-exchange and many-body effects inside the clock, so the physics content does not depend on a future deviation from the Standard Model being found. Five members converged on the same pair and the same division of credit, but I hold the position on the scientific evidence, not on that count. I would word the citation around the invention and the 10^-18 realisation only, and leave out any reference to the SI second and to prospective uses such as constants, geodesy and dark matter, so that the prize rests on what has been demonstrated.
statement.case_against: The objections I take seriously have not been removed. The novelty argument stands: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize honour the technical foundations of optical clocks, and a reader can call the lattice clock a refinement of a rewarded line. My answer is that those prizes gave the readout and the control tools, whereas the lattice clock is a different way of removing the trapping perturbation that limits neutral-atom clocks, but this is a judgement. The credit boundary is also soft: the invention can be argued as Katori's alone, Ye's contribution is performance and many-body physics rather than concept, and Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups made essential contributions that a two-name credit leaves out. Finally, no deviation from standard physics has been seen, so a committee that places discovery of nature above a new measurement capability could reasonably prefer B049 or B056. I disagree, but I cannot say that this view is unscientific.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the Higgs discovery is the clearest and most permanent result of fundamental physics in his working life, that the experimental half was left unrecognised in 2013, and that attribution to three of four ATLAS and CMS leaders is a judgement he cannot settle from the material.
responses.response: I do not dispute the scientific weight of the Higgs discovery, and I do not think the 2013 prize closes the question. My difficulty is the one you state yourself: a trio drawn from Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee drops a founder whichever way it is cut, and neither of us has a principled rule for the cut. On your discovery-versus-capability point, I would say that the lattice clock is not only a better number. It makes quantities observable that were not accessible before, for example the redshift across a millimetre and the collective behaviour of the atoms in the clock, and these have been shown, not promised. Where we differ is the weight to put on a clean two-name attribution against a larger discovery with a contested one. I keep B056 as an alternative because I would not call it a poor outcome, but I would not rank it above B008 unless the committee can state a rule for the three names that all of us accept.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B049, arguing that Kane and Mele's Z2 classification together with Molenkamp's observation of quantised edge transport in HgTe is a complete discovery, and asks whether it is better to wait on the lattice clock until the SI second is redefined.
responses.response: On waiting, I would answer no: a physics prize for a measurement capability that exists and is in use should not be tied to the schedule of a metrology body, and the redefinition would add a use, not evidence for the clock. On B049, I follow the theory-then-experiment logic and accept that the field is mature, but as an experimentalist I am bothered by the point you concede yourself, that the HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction and not the graphene model in the Kane-Mele paper, and that the edge-transport evidence is delicate. A citation that credits Kane and Mele for the concept and Molenkamp for the observation has to describe a link that the record does not quite make. If you and Mehlig can word it so that this is not misstated, I would regard B049 as the strongest of the non-clock options, which is why it is my first alternative. I do not agree that a new state of matter is automatically a stronger kind of achievement than a new way of measuring.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B008 first, says that the uncertainty budgets are credible from her own work on systematic shifts, and was asked by the chair whether any key systematic was established outside Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I cannot answer the chair's question on credit for the systematics better than you can, but from the laboratory side my recollection is as follows. The blackbody-radiation shift, which limits the accuracy at the 10^-18 level, was addressed by Ye's group in the JILA system and by Katori's group in a cryogenic Sr clock, and the lattice-induced hyperpolarisability and density shifts were examined by several groups, including NIST and PTB, for the operational magic wavelength. So the techniques are shared, and an uncertainty budget at this level is a community result. This does not change my view of who is credited, because the prize is for the idea and its leading realisation, but I think the citation should not say that Katori and Ye established every systematic. I ask you to correct me if the atomic-structure side differs, since I have not checked the primary papers here.

responses.point: Pearce, who opened with IceCube first, now proposes B008 and says the citation must name both the invention and the development so that Ye's part is not lost, while noting that a two-name prize leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow and Sterr.
responses.response: I agree that the citation should say invention and development, and I have adopted wording that names both, with the 10^-18 level as the demonstrated result. I would not add the phrase 'a new regime of precision measurement' from your wording, because it claims more than a citation should and it invites the question of what the new regime has yielded. On the groups outside the pair, my view is that the line is a judgement, but it is a defensible one: Katori made the invention and the first Sr lattice clock, and Ye's group took it to the accuracy and stability that convinced the other laboratories to follow. I also note that your IceCube alternative is secure on the existence of the astrophysical flux but less so on the sources, so I have not kept it among my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or as a refinement of that line. I judge it distinct but cannot settle this by experiment.

Whether the credit boundary around Katori and Ye is fair given the contributions of SYRTE, PTB, NIST and other laboratories to the systematics, which is a judgement from my recollection and not from a check of the primary papers.
Whether the committee gives greater weight to a discovery about nature than to a new measurement capability when no deviation from standard physics has been found.
Whether a two-part configuration is feasible: the three-person cap leaves one name for a second part, so I do not propose one.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD in the 1980s. Jun Ye is associated with the Hall/JILA group, but to my recollection he joined it much later, and I have no collaboration, joint publication or other tie with Katori or Ye. I disclosed this in round 1 and I leave it to the committee to decide whether recusal on B008 is needed; I am prepared to participate with the disclosure noted unless it prefers otherwise. I am in the leadership of WACQT, whose superconducting-qubit work relies on circuit QED (B012), and WACQT is tied institutionally to Chalmers, so I have dropped B012 from my alternatives and I do not press it.
